newsitem.title: FRANCE: France offers wage talks after one-day strike.
newsitem.headline: France offers wage talks after one-day strike.

text.p: France's centre-right government, rocked by a 24-hour public employees strike against its cuts and against record unemployment, has offered to meet unions for wage negotiations.
The centre-right administration played down the impact of Thursday's stoppage but offered to launch talks late this year, tackling one of the protesters' many demands.
Civil Service Minister Dominique Perben told TF1 television late on Thursday that only one in three civil servants had heeded the strike call, far less than during similar strikes last year.

But unions highlighted disruption to rail, air, school and postal services, and the fact that tens of thousands of demonstrators marched through cities across France -- more than in last year's protests by civil servants.

Many schools closed, domestic and short-haul flights were drastically reduced and only one train in three was running as a result of the first major labour protest since a crippling public sector strike lasting nearly four weeks in late 1995.
"There is no doubt this is a success. It's now up to the government to answer our grievances," said the Force Ouvriere union.
"We now have the momentum going, which will continue and grow stronger each day," echoed Louis Viannet, secretary general of the Communist-led CGT union.
"To build on the momentum created on this day of October 17, we urge all labour organisations to join with us in a new major initiative on around November 15," he told RTL radio.
Unions including the non-partisan Force Ouvriere and the pro-Socialist CFDT have called protests for coming weeks.
Perben offered to start negotiations as soon as the end of this year, saying that an economic upturn forecast by the government should help parties reach an agreement on wages.
"I'm convinced that from the month of December we will start talks to reach a wage agreement," he said, but acknowledged however that his margin of manoeuvre was narrow.

About half of France's teachers stayed away from work, as did about a third of postal and France Telecom staff, unions and the government said. Separately, many doctors refused to treat the sick in a protest over health care reforms.
But the Paris bus and Metro network operated close to normal, giving the impression of a city still ticking along, in contrast to the chaos of last year's 24-day transport strike.

"All together in defence of public service, jobs and purchasing power," read the banner at the head of a giant march that sprawled through central Paris. The CGT said 100,000 people took part but police put the number at about 23,000.

The strike was sparked by fears among five million public employees of job cuts under Prime Minister Alain Juppe's austerity drive to cut France's deficit in time for the planned single European Union currency in 1999.
Despite the big turnout, the Paris march highlighted old divisions in the labour movement over the social security reform which was one of the catalysts for last year's strike.
CGT marchers hurled abuse at Nicole Notat, whose CFDT union joined the stoppage though it backed Juppe's welfare reform plans and stayed out of last year's strikes.
Notat complained the doctors' strike was diverting the protest from its focus on the public sector.

Civil servants were protesting against government plans to trim their numbers by 6,000 next year. Teachers will bear the brunt of the austerity drive, with a loss of 2,300 permanent jobs and the layoff of around 15,000 short-term contract staff.

The strikes and demonstrations reflected widespread disenchantment with conservative President Jacques Chirac, elected in May 1995 after promising to make unemployment his top priority, to cut taxes and to allow higher wages.
